newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Africa can feed itself in 10 years, researcher.
newsitem.headline: Africa can feed itself in 10 years, researcher.

text.p: Africa, the world's poorest continent, should be able to feed its teeming population in the next decade, according to a leading agriculture researcher.

"If we really would organise things well and given proper political support, there is no reason why Africa should not be able to feed itself in 10 years," said Lukas Brader, director of the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA).

Brader, a Dutchman who heads the biggest agricultural research institute in Sub-Saharan Africa, told reporters at IITA's Ibadan base in southwestern Nigeria on Tuesday that farm output was already increasing in some African countries because of better crop varieties and improved management.
"If production would increase by three to four percent by the year 2000 then there would be almost an equilibrium to the demand and supply side of food," he added.

Food production in most African nations is rising by two percent annually but some countries like Ghana, Ivory Coast and Mauritius are already increasing output by an average of four percent annually.
"That gives us hope for the future," said Brader.
IITA was conceived by two American philantropic groups, the Ford and Rockefeller foundations, who provided the initial funding for the takeoff of the institute 30 years ago this week.
Since then it has expanded into a large lush green settlement on the edge of Ibadan, a chaotic city of three million people where local amenities are stretched.
Funding for the non-profit institution has come from a variety of sources including the United States, the Nordic countries and Japan to support an annual budget of $32 million.
Brader said the new challenge for scientists from nearly 40 different countries working at IITA was using biotechnology to create new varieties of crops that would be completely resistant to pests.

"We are employing biotechnology where there are recalcitrant problems and by the end of the year we will have important results," said George Thottappilly, an Indian who has been in Nigeria for 18 years and heads the biotechnology research unit.
His team of researchers are excited that already genes have been isolated in IITA laboratories and injected into cowpeas, banana and plantains to stiffen their resistance to pests.
"Our target is to get to farmers varieties that are fully resistant to pests and yield more," said Jesse Machuka, a Kenyan post-doctoral fellow at the unit.
"What it means is that farmers will be able to plant these varieties without bothering about having to apply insecticides," added Allesandra Pellegrineschi, an Italian biotechnologist.
Other crops targeted are tubers like cassava and yam, which are produced mostly in Africa to feed local populations and are becoming raw materials for local industries.
